newsitem.title: KUWAIT: Kurdish peace key to Iraq oil exports-Britain.
newsitem.headline: Kurdish peace key to Iraq oil exports-Britain.

text.p: British Foreign Office Minister Jeremy Hanley said on Tuesday Iraq could be allowed to export limited amounts of oil for the first time in six years if Kurdish groups ended fighting in northern Iraq.
"We have urged the two Kurdish parties to come together," Hanley told reporters in Kuwait before leaving for Qatar.
"I am very hopeful that should that occur...we will be able to have implemented Security Council resolution 986 which has been postponed because of that problem."

Iraq's May accord with the United Nations, known as the oil- for-food deal, would have allowed Iraq to sell $2 billion worth of oil over six months to pay for much needed imports and meet some 1990-91 Gulf crisis payments.
The deal was put on hold when Iraqi President Saddam Hussein sided militarily with one Kurdish group against the other in late August.
Iraq, once a key world oil exporter, has been under strict U.N. sanctions since Baghdad invaded Kuwait in 1990. A U.S.-led coalition defeated Iraq in the 1991 Gulf War.
Hanley said Kurdish factions should not fight each other but "they should look for what binds them together to share their struggles against their common enemy Saddam Hussein.

"There is no solution to their problems that allows Saddam Hussein to be the answer. He will be a further problem to them, therefore we urge them to meet to discuss and to bring peace between the two Kurdish factions."
